answer:
English is almost impossible to avoid in everyday life. We hear it on television and in song lyrics, study it at school, and, for many of us, use it at work. This constant exposure gives us a fairly good sense of how the language works. I think most people can understand at least some English, and quite a few probably have an excellent command of it. However, when I consider my own abilities, some areas are clearly more challenging than others. I feel more confident in the receptive skills of reading and listening, whereas writing and speaking are more difficult for me.

Throughout my years of studying English, first at primary school and then at secondary school, my teachers always emphasised writing. In upper secondary school in particular, we wrote many essays and various kinds of reviews. Even though I have had quite a lot of practice writing in English, I still encounter problems. Spelling can sometimes be difficult, of course, but grammar presents a greater challenge for me. In my experience, grammatical problems are often complicated and harder to resolve than spelling difficulties, which can usually be settled by looking up a word in a dictionary.

We did not get much reading practice at school. We had textbooks, of course, but the passages were often very short and covered unrelated topics, making them feel as though they had been taken out of context. In other words, the textbooks were boring. Besides these passages, we also read several works of literature and wrote reviews of them. I think reading literature is a tremendously rewarding way to develop proficiency in a language. This experience also proved very useful when I studied religious studies, as much of the required reading was in English.

My greatest difficulty when reading English arises when a text contains specialist language. Reading something that would probably be challenging even in Swedish is both demanding and time-consuming. This brings me to another problem with my reading: my patience, or rather, my lack of it. Naturally, reading a text in English takes longer than reading one in Swedish, at least initially, but for some reason I find that hard to accept.

Speaking and listening are obviously closely related. Even so, I find listening the easiest of the four skills and speaking the most difficult. This undoubtedly has to do with the fact that I get far more practice listening, especially through television and music, than speaking. Although I do not understand every word, I can usually follow what is being said. Specialist language, however, presents difficulties in listening just as it does in reading.

As I mentioned earlier, my biggest challenge in English is speaking. I have had little practical experience because I have never spent an extended period abroad. English teaching at school focused primarily, or even exclusively, on theory, so I had little opportunity to practise speaking there either. If anything, school can make you even more reluctant to speak: you become so concerned with getting the grammar right that you are afraid to open your mouth for fear of being laughed at. I know this sounds terrible, and it probably does not apply to everyone. Still, I believe these fears would fade quite quickly with regular speaking practice.

Having completed this assignment, I have realised how difficult it is to assess my own abilities in the four language skills. I have never had trouble getting good grades in English at school, but I firmly believe that grades rarely tell us much about what someone actually knows. What I do know is that learning a language involves many different skills, and I would like to improve in all of them.
